items.title: Agent node fire-and-forget mode spawns a standalone task and advances immediately
items.brief:
Symptom: an agent node's config accepts `fireAndForget: true` (the editor shows a "Fire and forget (don't wait for completion)" checkbox that promises "Creates a standalone task with its own chat. The flow advances immediately. Chain depth limited to 5", flow validation accepts the boolean, and the agent output schema documents `spawnedTaskId` and `fireAndForget` outputs). But the local agent dispatcher ignores the flag: a fire-and-forget agent node still creates a flow-linked task that continues the start_task's chat, links that chat to the task, and pauses the run with `awaiting_input` until the agent finishes, exactly like a normal agent node. Dispatching the same fire-and-forget node run twice also has no defined result.

Required behaviour, when an agent node's config has `fireAndForget: true` (only the boolean `true` counts; anything else keeps today's behaviour unchanged):
1. All existing validation still applies first and returns the same errors (for example `{ type: 'error', message: 'agent missing instructions' }`), and creates no task row: missing instructions, missing flow run/version, no completed upstream start_task with a projectId, missing chatId/subChatId, and the chain-depth refusal when the incoming `triggerContext._flowChainDepth` is 5 or more.
2. The dispatcher creates exactly one new task row for the project of the upstream start_task. Its description is built the same way as for a normal agent node (optional "## Role" prefix from agentInstructions, then the rendered instructions, with {{previous.*}} / {{trigger.*}} / loop variables rendered). Its title is the upstream start_task label, or "Flow: Agent" when there is none.
3. The task is standalone: it is not linked to the flow run or node run (`tasks.flowRunId` and `tasks.nodeRunId` are both null), so its completion can never advance, pause or fail the flow. Its trigger context must not ask to continue the start_task's chat: `triggerContext._config.executionMode` is not `'continue_chat'` and `triggerContext._config.continueChatId` is absent, so the task runs in a chat of its own.
3a. Like a normal agent task, the spawned task still receives the flow's settings: when the flow version has a non-empty `graph.settings.briefing`, `triggerContext._config.flowBriefing` holds it rendered against `{{trigger.*}}`; an agent-level `model` override appears as `triggerContext._config.model`.
4. The chain-depth bookkeeping still applies to the spawned task: `triggerContext._flowChainDepth` equals the incoming depth plus 1 (incoming depth 0 when absent), and `triggerContext._flowOriginId` equals the flow run id.
5. The start_task's chat is not linked to the spawned task: `chats.taskId` of the upstream chat stays as it was (null stays null).
6. The dispatcher returns `{ type: 'completed', output }` where `output.status === 'completed'` and `output.outputs` includes `spawnedTaskId` (the new task's id) and `fireAndForget: true`. It must not return `awaiting_input`.
7. Dispatching the same node run again (same `nodeRunId`) does not create a second task and does not throw; it returns the same completed result with the same `spawnedTaskId`.

Interface: `dispatchAgent` exported from `src/main/lib/flows/dispatch/agent.ts` (the existing `Dispatcher` signature), the task rows in the `tasks` table (`id`, `projectId`, `title`, `description`, `flowRunId`, `nodeRunId`, `triggerContext`), and the `taskId` column of the upstream chat row.

items.title: Enforce condition loop limits (loop.maxIterations / onMaxReached) in the local engine
items.brief:
Symptom: a condition node may originate a back-edge, forming a loop, and its config accepts `loop: { maxIterations: number, onMaxReached?: "fail" | "continue" }` (validated as an integer 1-50; the editor defaults it to 10 / "fail"; the Flow guidelines promise "Loop maxIterations is 1-50; there is also an engine per-node iteration guard (default 10)"). The local engine ignores all of this: when a condition keeps choosing its looping edge, the loop body is re-dispatched forever, and `onMaxReached` has no effect.

Definitions:
- A condition node's "loop edge" is one of its outgoing edges that closes a cycle in the flow graph: its target is a node from which the condition can be reached again by following edges. Its other outgoing edge is the "exit edge".
- The node's limit N is `config.loop.maxIterations` when it is an integer from 1 to 50; otherwise (loop missing, or an invalid value) N is 10. The action on reaching it is `config.loop.onMaxReached` when that is `"continue"`, otherwise `"fail"`.
- An "iteration" is one time the engine follows the condition's loop edge within the same flow run.

Required behaviour when a condition node finishes in a flow run and its result selects the loop edge:
1. If that condition has followed its loop edge fewer than N times so far in this flow run, the engine follows the loop edge exactly as today.
2. Otherwise the limit is reached and the loop edge is NOT followed:
   - action "fail": the flow run's status becomes `failed`, no further node run is created, and a `run_failed` flow event is emitted whose `summary` is exactly `Condition "<label>" reached its loop limit (<N> iterations)`, where <label> is the node's `label`, or its `id` when it has no label.
   - action "continue": the engine follows the exit edge instead, as if the condition had selected it (so when the exit edge leads to an `end` node, that node runs once and the run completes as it does today). If there is no exit edge, the run completes (`completed`, `run_completed`).
3. A condition whose selected edge is not a loop edge, and conditions without a loop edge, behave exactly as today. So a loop with N = 3 whose condition always selects the loop edge dispatches the loop body 4 times in total (the first pass plus 3 iterations) and evaluates the condition 4 times before the limit applies.

Interface: `dispatchAndAdvance` and `loadRunContext` exported from `src/main/lib/flows/advance.ts` (existing signatures), `subscribeFlowEvents` from `src/main/lib/flows/events.ts`, and the `flow_runs` / `node_runs` rows (`status`, `nodeId`). The engine runs every node, conditions included, only through `dispatchNode` from `src/main/lib/flows/dispatch`, and the limit must hold whatever result `dispatchNode` returns for a condition. Condition results use the existing shape: `outputs.result` is `'continue'` (follows the `sourceHandle: "true"` edge) or `'stop'` (follows the `"false"` edge).

items.title: Batch stage definition: validate the whole DAG, resolve dependencies across calls, allow redefining pending stages
Garbage-collect leftover Fan Out iteration state for runs that can no longer resume
items.brief:
Symptom: while a Fan Out iterates, the engine keeps per-run rows in the `flow_kv_state` table under two key shapes: `_fanOut:<flowRunId>:<fanOutNodeId>` (the iteration state) and `_fanOutBodyMember:<flowRunId>:<bodyNodeId>` (one per body node). They are removed only when the Fan Out finishes all items. A run that stops part-way through (cancelled by the user, cancelled because its chat was removed, or deleted) leaves those rows behind forever, one set per run, and nothing ever cleans them up.

Required behaviour: two new exports from `src/main/lib/flows/fan-out-state.ts`.

1. `cleanupFanOutStateForRun(flowId: string, flowRunId: string): Promise<number>` deletes every `flow_kv_state` row of flow `flowId` whose key is exactly `_fanOut:<flowRunId>:<anything>` or `_fanOutBodyMember:<flowRunId>:<anything>`, and returns how many rows it deleted. It must not delete any other row: not rows of other runs (including a run whose id merely starts with the same characters, e.g. `run1` vs `run10`), not rows of other flows, and not keys that only look similar (for example `xfanOut:<flowRunId>:n`, `fanOut:<flowRunId>:n`, or `_fanOut_<flowRunId>:n`; underscores and percent signs in keys are literal characters, never wildcards).

2. `sweepStaleFanOutState(): Promise<number>` looks at every Fan Out row in `flow_kv_state` (keys starting with `_fanOut:` or `_fanOutBodyMember:`; the flow run id is the text between the first and second `:`) and deletes the rows whose flow run can no longer resume, returning how many rows it deleted. A run can no longer resume when:
   - no `flow_runs` row with that id exists; or
   - the run's status is `completed`; or
   - the run's status is `cancelled` and none of its node runs is a restart interruption. A node run is a restart interruption when its stored output's `error.message` equals `RESTART_INTERRUPTION_REASON` (exported from `src/shared/types/flow.ts`, value `Interrupted by app restart`).
   Rows of runs that are `pending`, `running`, `paused` or `failed`, and of cancelled runs that do have a restart-interrupted node run, are kept (those runs can still be retried or carried on). Non-Fan Out keys are never touched.

3. The sweep runs once as part of the app's boot recovery, best-effort (a failure is logged, never thrown to the caller).

Interface: `cleanupFanOutStateForRun`, `sweepStaleFanOutState`, and the existing `saveFanOutState`, `saveBodyMembers`, `loadFanOutState`, `loadBodyMember` from `src/main/lib/flows/fan-out-state.ts`; `setKv` / `getKv` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/flow-kv-state.ts`; `RESTART_INTERRUPTION_REASON` from `src/shared/types/flow.ts`; the `flow_runs.status` and `node_runs.nodeOutput` columns.

items.title: Post-task trigger: honour status and source filters, skip history, and fill the documented trigger fields
items.brief:
Symptom: the post-task trigger editor saves `triggerStates` (default `['done', 'completed']`, or `['all']`) and an optional `filterBySource` list into the binding's `config`, and the trigger schema tells flow authors they can read `{{trigger.source}}`, `{{trigger.result}}`, `{{trigger.branch}}`, `{{trigger.baseBranch}}`, `{{trigger.worktreePath}}`, `{{trigger.chatId}}` and `{{trigger.projectPath}}`. The local poller ignores the binding config entirely: it starts a run for every terminal task in the project whatever its status or source, including tasks that finished long before the binding existed (so enabling a binding starts one run per historical task), and the trigger context it passes carries only `_frinkTrigger`, `bindingId`, `taskId`, `projectId`, `taskStatus`, `taskTitle` and `taskCompletedAt`.

Required behaviour of one poll pass, `runPostTaskTriggerTick(): Promise<{ fired: number; skipped: number }>`, which must be exported from `src/main/lib/flows/post-task-trigger.ts`. For each active `post_task_trigger` binding and each task of the binding's project whose `completedAt` is set:
1. Status filter. Read `binding.config.triggerStates`. Valid entries are `done`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`, `needs_attention`, `plan_ready`, `all`; other values are ignored. If the array is missing, not an array, or has no valid entries, it means `['done', 'completed']`. If it contains `all`, every one of the six task statuses above matches. Otherwise the task's status must be one of the listed states. A non-matching task does not start a run and is not counted as fired.
2. Source filter. Read `binding.config.filterBySource`. If it is a non-empty array of strings (entries trimmed, empty entries dropped), the task's `source` must equal one of the entries, compared case-insensitively; otherwise any source matches.
3. History. A task only matches when its `completedAt` is at or after the binding's `createdAt`.
4. Matching tasks start a run exactly as today (same flow, idempotency key `post_task:<bindingId>:<taskId>`, one run per binding and task across passes), with these trigger context fields added to the existing ones:
   - `source`: the task's `source`;
   - `result`: `task.result.agentSignal.summary` when that is a string, otherwise `null`;
   - `chatId`, `branch`, `baseBranch`, `worktreePath`: taken from the chat linked to the task (the `chats` row whose `taskId` is the task id; the most recently created one if several), each `null` when absent or when no chat is linked;
   - `projectPath`: the `path` of the task's project row, or `null`.
5. The return value counts `fired` (runs started this pass) and `skipped` (matching pairs not started because they already fired or starting failed); pairs rejected by rules 1-3 are counted in neither.

Interface: `runPostTaskTriggerTick` and the existing `stopPostTaskTriggerLoop` from `src/main/lib/flows/post-task-trigger.ts` (`stopPostTaskTriggerLoop()` keeps clearing the poller's in-memory record of fired pairs, while within one poller lifetime a second pass must not start a pair again); runs are started only through `startFlowRun({ flowId, triggerContext, idempotencyKey })` from `src/main/lib/flows/start.ts`; all database reads go through `getDatabase()` from `src/main/lib/db` (a fresh in-memory database made with `freshDb` from `src/main/lib/db/test-utils/fresh-db.ts` behaves the same); the binding repo `create` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/flow-trigger-bindings.ts` (fields `flowId`, `projectId`, `triggerType: 'post_task_trigger'`, `config`, `isActive`, `createdAt`); and rows inserted directly into the `projects`, `flows`, `tasks` and `chats` tables from `src/main/lib/db/schema` (`tasks.projectId`, `title`, `status`, `source`, `completedAt`, `result`; `chats.projectId`, `taskId`, `worktreePath`, `branch`, `baseBranch`; `projects.path`). Example values: a second pass over the same two matching tasks returns `{ fired: 0, skipped: 2 }`; a task completed before the binding's `createdAt` returns `{ fired: 0, skipped: 0 }`.

items.title: Adding batch stage runs: pending stages only, per-run trigger validation reported per run
items.brief:
Symptom: `addStageRuns(flowId, stageNumber, batchId, runs)` (behind the `frink_flows_add_stage_runs` tool, documented as "pending stages only" and "Per-run errors are reported without aborting the whole call") appends runs to any stage whatever its status, so runs can be added to a stage that is already running, completed, failed or cancelled, where they are never dispatched or silently change a settled stage. It also accepts any trigger context: a run whose context has a value of the wrong type for a variable the flow declares in `graph.settings.batchTriggerSchema`, or a context larger than the documented 10,000-character limit, is stored as if valid and only fails (or misbehaves) much later when the batch dispatches it.

Required behaviour of `addStageRuns(flowId, stageNumber, batchId, runs)` exported from `src/main/lib/flows/mcp-cloud-shim.ts` (return shape unchanged: `{ added: Array<{ runId, index }>, failed: Array<{ index, error }> }`, where `index` is the position in `runs` and `runId` is the new batch stage run id):
1. Unknown stage number: unchanged (throws `TRPCError` code `NOT_FOUND`, message `Batch <batchId> has no stage with number <stageNumber>`).
2. If the stage's status is not `pending`, the call throws a `TRPCError` with code `PRECONDITION_FAILED` and message `Stage <stageNumber> is <status>; runs can only be added to a pending stage`, and no run is added.
3. More than 50 runs in one call throws a `TRPCError` with code `BAD_REQUEST` and message `At most 50 runs can be added per call`, and no run is added.
4. Each run is checked on its own before it is stored; a run that fails a check is reported in `failed` with that exact message and not stored, while the other runs of the call are still added:
   - When `JSON.stringify(triggerContext)` is longer than 10000 characters: `triggerContext exceeds 10000 characters`.
   - When a key declared in the flow's `graph.settings.batchTriggerSchema` is present (not undefined/null) with the wrong type: the same message the batch dispatcher already uses, `trigger.<key> expected <type>, got <actual>` (`<actual>` is `array` for arrays, otherwise `typeof`). Declared types are `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `object` (a non-array, non-null object) and `array`. The schema is read from the flow version the batch runs against: the version of the batch's earliest flow run if it has one, otherwise the flow's latest version.
   - A run with no trigger context passes both checks.
5. Valid runs are stored as today: status `pending`, trigger context as given (or null).

Interface: `addStageRuns` and `defineFlowBatchStages(flowId, batchId, [{ stageNumber: 1, runs: [] }])` from `src/main/lib/flows/mcp-cloud-shim.ts`, `listRunsForStage(db, stageId)` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/batch-stage-runs.ts`, `listStagesForBatch(db, batchId)` / `setStageStatusIf(db, stageId, 'pending', <status>)` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/batch-stages.ts`, `createFlow` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/flows.ts` and `createFlowVersion` from `src/main/lib/db/repos/flow-versions.ts` (graph `{ nodes: [], edges: [], settings }`, where `settings.batchTriggerSchema` is an array of `{ key, type }`), rows inserted into the `flowRuns` table from `src/main/lib/db/schema` (`flowVersionId`, `status`, `batchId`, `createdAt`) to pin a batch to an older version, and `TRPCError` from `@trpc/server`. All database access goes through `getDatabase()` from `src/main/lib/db` (a fresh in-memory database built by `freshDb` from `src/main/lib/db/test-utils/fresh-db.ts` behaves the same). Example values: a context whose `JSON.stringify` is exactly 10000 characters is added and one of 10001 characters is reported; exactly 50 runs in one call are all added.

items.title: Let a person reject a paused approval step, ending the run
Startup worktree recovery also reclaims dead stubs under per-project base-path overrides
items.brief:
Symptom: at startup Frink runs `recoverOrphanedWorktrees(db, worktreeBaseDir)`, exported from src/main/lib/trpc/routers/chats/teardown-worktree.ts. It deletes leftover `<base>/<project-slug>/<folder>` directories that git has forgotten, but only under the one global base it is passed. A project can set its own worktree base with the `worktree-base-path` key in `<projectPath>/.frink/worktrees.json`, and Frink then creates that project's chat worktrees there. Dead leftover directories under such a per-project base are never reclaimed, so they leak on disk forever.

Required behaviour for `recoverOrphanedWorktrees(db, worktreeBaseDir)`:
1. It sweeps the global `worktreeBaseDir` exactly as today. An empty string still means the global base is not swept. It also sweeps the per-project override base of every registered project that has a path. A project's override base is the `worktree-base-path` value in that project's `.frink/worktrees.json`, normalised with `normalizeWorktreeBasePath` and honoured only when `isSafeConfiguredWorktreeBasePath(value)` returns true. Both functions live in src/main/lib/worktree/base-path-validation.ts and must be the ones that make this decision. A missing, unreadable or invalid config file (for example text that is not JSON, or a `worktree-base-path` that is not a string), or an unsafe value, means that project has no override. A project's override is swept even when git lists no worktrees for that project (for example, when the project is not a git repo).
2. Each distinct normalised base is swept at most once per call. Two projects that share an override, or an override equal to the global base, cause one sweep of that directory.
3. Override bases use the same removal rules as the global sweep. A `<base>/<slug>/<folder>` directory is removed only when all three hold: no non-archived chat's worktreePath or registered project path equals it; git does not list it for any project; and it has no live `.git` linkage (as decided by the exported `hasLiveGitLinkage`). A slug directory left empty is removed too. One unreadable or locked directory never aborts the rest.
4. The returned `orphaned` is the total number of directories removed across all swept bases. The result object gains a new field, `sweptBases: string[]`. It lists every base actually swept, each once, with the global base first (as passed) when it is non-empty, followed by override bases in their normalised form (for example, an override written as `/x/wt/` is listed as `/x/wt`). With no global base and no overrides it is `[]`.
5. With `FRINK_DISABLE_WORKTREE_RECOVERY=1` the function still returns `{ pruned: 0, removed: 0, skipped: 0, orphaned: 0 }` and touches nothing. `sweptBases` is `[]` in that case.

The existing tests of this function keep passing; the only change they need is that expectations of the result's exact shape now include `sweptBases`.

items.title: Instruction files get a capability row with a report-only delivery probe
items.brief:
Symptom: Frink's provider spine (the `project()` interface exported from src/main/lib/provider/index.ts) describes each provider with a capability row. It has no category for instruction files (project `AGENTS.md`, user-global `CLAUDE.md`), so nothing can be asked whether the user's instructions reached a run. Frink does feed them to Claude Code: it injects the project's `AGENTS.md` into the system prompt and copies `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` into the session config. But an `AGENTS.md` over 100 KiB is silently skipped, and nothing reports it. The standing rule (docs/decisions/provider-config-canonical-home.md, Target 2026-07-26, corrections 2 and 3) is that instructions is a real category, and a category with no row cannot be probed.

Required behaviour:
1. Every capability row gains the key `instructions`, whose value is a capability mode like the other keys, and `'instructions'` becomes a category that `deliver` and `enforce` accept. The rows in `CAPABILITY_MAP` (exported from src/main/lib/provider/capabilities.ts) are `'claude-code': 'inject'` and `'none'` for `cursor`, `codex`, `gemini` and `opencode`. `getCapabilityDescriptor` (same module) of an unknown provider also gives `'none'`. No other key is added and no other existing mode changes.
2. `project(projectId, projectPath, provider).deliver('instructions')` for `claude-code` returns a report-only `DispatchResult`, with `category: 'instructions'` and `mode: 'inject'`. It creates and modifies no files. It reads two files, at the time of the call:
   - The project file `<projectPath>/AGENTS.md` counts as present when it exists, its content is not only whitespace, and its size is at most 102400 bytes. If it exists, is not blank and is larger than 102400 bytes, the call returns `status: 'noop'` with `detail` exactly `'DELIVERY FAILURE — project AGENTS.md is larger than 102400 bytes and is not injected'` (the separator is an em dash, U+2014), whether or not the user file exists.
   - The user file `<home>/.claude/CLAUDE.md` counts as present when it exists. `<home>` is the value of the `FRINK_HOME` environment variable, trimmed, when it is set and not blank, otherwise the OS home directory; it is read at the time of each call.
   - When there is no failure and at least one file is present, the result is `status: 'delivered'` with `detail` naming the present files, joined by `', '` in this order: `'project AGENTS.md'`, `'user CLAUDE.md'`. For example, `'project AGENTS.md, user CLAUDE.md'`.
   - When neither is present, the result is `status: 'noop'` with `detail: 'no instruction files'`.
   The result object has exactly the keys `category`, `mode`, `status` and `detail`.
3. For providers whose `instructions` mode is `'none'`, `deliver('instructions')` keeps the existing generic answer `{ category: 'instructions', mode: 'none', status: 'noop', detail: 'not bridged for this provider' }`. `enforce('instructions')` for claude-code returns the existing deliver-only answer: category `'instructions'`, mode `'inject'`, status `'noop'`, detail `'deliver mode — use deliver()'`.

The existing tests keep passing; the only change they need is that expectations of a whole capability row now include `instructions`.

items.title: Kept local edits to Frink-shipped skills surface as an in-app notice
items.brief:
Symptom: at startup Frink provisions its shipped skills (today `frink-flows`) into the user's Frink skills directory. When a shipped update arrives and the user has edited some of the skill's files, Frink keeps those edited files and updates the rest. When a user copy has no `.baseline.json`, Frink refuses to touch it. In both cases the only signal is a `log.warn` line. The user never learns that their edited copy (possibly an edited `SKILL.md` that now contradicts the updated references) is out of step with the shipped version, or how to take the shipped version. docs/decisions/frink-flows-skill-source-of-truth.md (2026-09-14 note) records the in-app notice as an open follow-up (sc-2232).

Required behaviour:
1. `ProvisionOutcome` (exported from src/main/lib/skills/skill-provisioner.ts) gains an optional `keptEdits?: string[]`. Whenever a skill's outcome has status `'preserved-user-edits'` because locally edited files were kept, `keptEdits` lists their skill-relative paths (for example `'SKILL.md'`, `'references/nodes.md'`), sorted ascending by plain string comparison (code-unit order, so `'SKILL.md'` comes before `'references/a.md'`). For the "no .baseline.json in the user copy" refusal it is `[]`. For every other status the key is absent.
2. A notice store with these exports from `src/main/lib/skills/index.ts`:
   - `type SkillEditNotice = { skill: string; reason: 'kept-edits' | 'no-baseline'; keptEdits: string[]; skillMdKept: boolean }`
   - `listSkillEditNotices(): SkillEditNotice[]`, sorted by `skill`. It returns copies: changing the returned array, a returned notice or a notice's `keptEdits` array does not change the store.
   - `dismissSkillEditNotice(skill: string): boolean`. It removes that skill's notice and returns true when there was one, otherwise false.
3. Each provisioning of a skill updates that skill's notice from its outcome. This applies to every provisioning of that skill, whether through `provisionFrinkSkills()` or the per-skill `__test__.provisionOne(skillName, sourceRoot)` already exported from src/main/lib/skills/skill-provisioner.ts.
   - A shipped update that was applied while keeping edited files (the case that logs the "updated … but kept N locally edited file(s)" warning) sets the notice `{ skill, reason: 'kept-edits', keptEdits, skillMdKept: keptEdits.includes('SKILL.md') }`.
   - The no-baseline refusal sets `{ skill, reason: 'no-baseline', keptEdits: [], skillMdKept: false }`.
   - An outcome of `'installed'`, `'updated'` or `'unchanged'` clears that skill's notice.
   - A `'preserved-user-edits'` outcome where nothing shipped was written, because only the kept files differ, still reports `keptEdits` on the outcome but leaves any existing notice as it is (including "none" after a dismissal). This keeps a dismissed notice dismissed until the next shipped change.
   - `'failed'` and `'no-source'` leave the notice unchanged.
4. The skills tRPC router, `skillsRouter` exported from src/main/lib/trpc/routers/skills.ts (the router whose procedures include `copyAcross` and `getAggregatedSkillInfo`), gains a query `listEditNotices` (no input) that returns `listSkillEditNotices()`, and a mutation `dismissEditNotice` with input `{ skill: string }` that returns `{ dismissed: boolean }`, where `dismissed` is the result of `dismissSkillEditNotice(skill)`.
5. The Skills settings surface shows each notice in plain words: which skill, which files were kept (calling out SKILL.md when it is among them), and that deleting a file and restarting Frink takes the shipped version. Each notice has a Dismiss control that calls `dismissEditNotice`.

Existing tests keep passing.

items.title: Export and import permission rules as a portable file
items.brief:
Symptom: a user's permission rules (strings such as `Bash(npm test:*)` or `Read`, each allow, deny or ask) live only in Frink's local database, per project or per machine. Rules can be added and removed only one at a time. There is no way to copy a project's rule set to another project or machine, or to back it up and restore it.

Required behaviour:
1. New module `src/main/lib/permissions/v2/rules-bundle.ts` with these exports:
   - `type RulesTarget = { scope: 'project'; projectId: string } | { scope: 'user' }`
   - `type PermissionRulesBundle = { format: 'frink-permission-rules'; version: 1; rules: Array<{ rule: string; type: 'allow' | 'deny' | 'ask' }> }`
   - `exportRulesBundle(db, target: RulesTarget): Promise<PermissionRulesBundle>`. It returns every stored rule of that scope (for a project, only that project's rules): all allow rules, then all deny rules, then all ask rules. Within each type the order is the stored order, the same order the existing `getProjectDoc` / `getUserDoc` return. Policy-file rules are never exported. An empty scope gives `{ format: 'frink-permission-rules', version: 1, rules: [] }`.
   - `importRulesBundle(db, input: unknown, target: RulesTarget): Promise<ImportRulesResult>`, where
     `type ImportRulesResult = { ok: true; added: number; duplicates: number } | { ok: false; error: 'format'; message: string } | { ok: false; error: 'invalid'; invalid: Array<{ index: number; message: string }> }`.
   `db` is the drizzle handle the functions in src/main/lib/permissions/v2/store-local.ts take (`ReturnType<typeof getDatabase>`; an in-memory database from `freshDb()` in src/main/lib/db/test-utils/fresh-db.ts works the same way).
2. Import rules:
   - If `input` is not an object with `format === 'frink-permission-rules'`, `version === 1` and an array `rules`, the result is `{ ok: false, error: 'format', message }` (message non-empty) and nothing is written. `null`, an array, a wrong `format`, a `version` other than 1 and a missing `rules` are all format errors.
   - Every entry must be an object with a string `rule` and a `type` of `'allow'`, `'deny'` or `'ask'`, and must pass `validateRuleString(rule, type)` from src/shared/lib/validate-rule.ts (the validator that adding a single rule already uses). If any entry fails, the result is `{ ok: false, error: 'invalid', invalid }`. `invalid` lists every failing entry by its zero-based index, in index order. Each `message` is non-empty: the validator's message when the validator rejected the entry, or a message of your own for a shape error (not an object, `rule` not a string, unknown `type`). Nothing at all is written in this case, not even the valid entries.
   - Otherwise each rule is stored trimmed in the target scope. `added` counts rules newly stored. `duplicates` counts entries skipped because the same (trimmed rule, type) already existed in that scope or appeared earlier in the same bundle. The same rule string with a different type is a different rule. `added + duplicates` equals the number of entries.
   - Importing into a project touches only that project's rules. Importing into user scope touches only user rules.
   - Exporting a project and importing the result into an empty project leaves the two projects with equal `getProjectDoc` results; importing the same bundle again gives `{ ok: true, added: 0, duplicates: <number of entries> }`.
3. The permissions tRPC router `permissionsRouter` (the one with `listProjectRules` and `addProjectRule`) gains a query `exportRules` with input `RulesTarget` that returns `exportRulesBundle`'s result, and a mutation `importRules` with input `{ target: RulesTarget; bundle: unknown }` that returns `importRulesBundle`'s result. Like the router's other procedures, they work on the database returned by `getDatabase()`; they are called through `permissionsRouter.createCaller({ getWindow: () => null })`.

Rules are set up and read back with the existing `addProjectRule`, `addUserRule`, `getProjectDoc` and `getUserDoc` from store-local. Existing tests must keep passing.

items.title: Auto-import MCP servers from Claude Code's per-project config and from Codex
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. Frink's silent MCP auto-import scans three places: `~/.claude.json` root `mcpServers` (source 'claude-global'), `~/.cursor/mcp.json` ('cursor-global') and each registered project's `<project>/.cursor/mcp.json` ('cursor-project'). Two native sources are never read: the servers Claude Code keeps per project in `~/.claude.json` under `projects[<projectPath>].mcpServers`, and the servers Codex keeps in its `config.toml` under `[mcp_servers.<name>]`. The user docs say Codex's native config "is not an import source yet", and the scanner says per-project Claude servers are "deferred to a follow-up".

(2) Required behaviour.
- The exported `ImportSource` type gains two values, `'claude-project'` and `'codex-global'`, and every place that types an import provenance or tombstone `source` accepts them.
- `scanNativeMcpSources()` also returns:
  a) Claude per-project candidates: for each registered Frink project (the same list the Cursor per-project scan uses) whose `path` is exactly a key of `projects` in `~/.claude.json`, one candidate per entry of that key's `mcpServers`: `{ name, source: 'claude-project', sourcePath: <frinkUserHome()>/.claude.json, projectPath: <the project path>, config: <the raw server object>, credentials }`, with `credentials` extracted exactly as for the other sources (`env`, `headers`, `_oauth` -> `oauth`). Projects in `~/.claude.json` that are not registered, or have no or empty `mcpServers`, yield nothing. If the local database cannot be read, these candidates are skipped and everything else is still returned.
  b) Codex candidates from the Codex config file: `<CODEX_HOME>/config.toml` when the `CODEX_HOME` environment variable is set and non-empty, otherwise `<frinkUserHome()>/.codex/config.toml`. One candidate per table under `mcp_servers` (`[mcp_servers.<name>]`; the name may be a quoted key such as `[mcp_servers."figma-remote"]`): `{ name, source: 'codex-global', sourcePath: <that file path>, config, credentials }` where `config` carries `command` (string), `args` (string array) and `url` (string) when present, and `credentials` carries `env` (from an `env` inline table or a `[mcp_servers.<name>.env]` sub-table) and `headers` (from an `http_headers` inline table, plus `Authorization: 'Bearer <value>'` when `bearer_token_env_var` names an environment variable that is set; nothing is added when it is unset). A credentials key with nothing in it is left out. A server with `enabled = false` is skipped. The file uses ordinary TOML: `#` comments, blank lines, basic double-quoted strings, arrays of strings, inline tables with quoted or bare keys, and other top-level keys and tables that are not `mcp_servers` (ignored). A missing or unparseable file yields no Codex candidates and does not affect the other sources.
  Frink's own loopback server names (`FRINK_OWNED_MCP_SERVERS`, e.g. `frink_dynamic_chat`) are skipped for both new sources, as for the others.
- `runMcpImporter()` keeps today's rules for a name found in more than one place (the first candidate in scan order is written, it counts as a conflict and no credentials are stored). New: when the written candidate's source is `'claude-project'`, the name is added once to `config.projects[<its projectPath>].mcps`, exactly as already happens for `'cursor-project'`.
- `candidateToFrinkConfig(c)` sets `description` to `Imported from Claude Code (<projectPath>)` for a `'claude-project'` candidate and `Imported from Codex` for a `'codex-global'` candidate, and `importedFrom.source` / `importedFrom.sourcePath` to the candidate's `source` / `sourcePath`.
- When a legacy entry (no `importedFrom`) is stamped by structural match, the preferred source order is: 'claude-global', 'cursor-global', 'codex-global', 'claude-project', 'cursor-project'.

(3) Interface. `scanNativeMcpSources(): Promise<ImportCandidate[]>` and the types `ImportSource`, `ImportCandidate` from `src/main/lib/mcp/import-scanner.ts` (candidate fields `name`, `source`, `sourcePath`, `projectPath`, `config`, `credentials`); `runMcpImporter(): Promise<{ imported: number; conflicts: number; backfilled: number }>`, `candidateToFrinkConfig(c)` and `_resetMcpImporterForTests()` from `src/main/lib/mcp/importer.ts`. Written config fields read back: `servers[name].description`, `servers[name].importedFrom.source`, `projects[path].mcps`, `deletedImports`; credentials file `servers[name]`. Files are read with `node:fs/promises` `readFile`; `~/.claude.json` is available both through `readClaudeConfig()` (src/main/lib/claude-config.ts) and through `readFile` on `<frinkUserHome()>/.claude.json`, and either may be used. Registered projects come from `listProjects(getDatabase())` (src/main/lib/db/repos/projects.ts and src/main/lib/db), as for the Cursor per-project scan; when that call fails, the Codex and global candidates are still returned. The importer keeps writing the config and credentials files through the existing `updateMcpConfigAtomic` and `updateMcpCredentialsAtomic` from src/main/lib/mcp/config.ts, keeps checking `safeStorage.isEncryptionAvailable()` from `electron`, and keeps using `resolveUserId()` (src/main/lib/machine) to decide on cloud sync. Existing tests must keep passing.

items.title: Terminal tabs show the last command the user ran
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. Terminal tabs are always labelled "Terminal 1", "Terminal 2" and so on, whatever the user runs in them, so with several terminals open the user cannot tell which one is running the dev server and which one is running tests.

(2) Required behaviour. When the user presses Enter on a command in a terminal, that terminal's tab (and anywhere else the terminal's name is shown, such as the split-pane header and sidebar) shows the cleaned command as its title. A later command replaces it. A command that cleans to an empty string leaves the title unchanged. Once the user renames a terminal by hand, the hand-given name always wins and later commands no longer change what the tab shows. Titles persist with the rest of the terminal list.

(3) Interface and exact values. `TerminalInstance` in `src/renderer/features/terminal/types.ts` gains two optional fields: `commandTitle?: string` and `hasCustomName?: boolean`. Add a new module `src/renderer/features/terminal/terminal-titles.ts` exporting:

- `applyCommandTitle(terminals: Record<string, TerminalInstance[]>, paneId: string, command: string): Record<string, TerminalInstance[]>` - cleans `command` for display: first removes ANSI escape sequences of the form ESC (U+001B) followed by `[`, then zero or more digits or semicolons, then one ASCII letter; then removes the remaining control characters (U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F); then trims surrounding whitespace; and finally cuts anything longer than 50 characters to its first 47 characters plus `...`. If the cleaned title is empty, if no terminal in any chat has `paneId === paneId`, or if the matching terminal's `commandTitle` already equals the cleaned title, it returns the very same `terminals` object (reference-equal). Otherwise it returns a new record in which only the matching terminal is replaced by a copy with `commandTitle` set to the cleaned title (all its other fields unchanged); every other terminal object and every other chat's list are the very same objects as in the input (reference-equal), and the input is not mutated. A later command replaces an earlier title.
- `getTerminalDisplayName(terminal: TerminalInstance): string` - returns `terminal.name` when `hasCustomName` is `true`; otherwise returns `commandTitle` when it is a non-empty string; otherwise returns `terminal.name`.
- `renameTerminalInstance(terminals: TerminalInstance[], id: string, name: string): TerminalInstance[]` - returns a new array in which the terminal with that `id` has `name` set to `name` and `hasCustomName: true` (its `commandTitle` is kept); other entries are the very same objects as in the input (reference-equal); neither the input array nor its objects are mutated. Unknown `id` returns an array equal to the input.

Existing tests must keep passing.

items.title: In-chat search finds text inside tool calls
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. The in-chat search bar (Cmd+F in a chat) only finds text in plain message text. A command the agent ran, a file it read or edited, or an error printed by a shell command is invisible to search, so searching a chat for `npm test` or for a file name the agent edited reports no matches even when that text is on screen inside a tool card.

(2) Required behaviour. Search also covers the tool-call fields listed below in assistant messages. Those matches are counted in the match total, and stepping through matches visits them in message order. In the Bash tool card, matches in the command, the output and the error text are highlighted like matches in message text, with the current match shown as current, and when the current match lies in a collapsed output area, that area expands so the match is visible. Highlighting inside the other tool cards is not required. User messages and plain assistant text are searched exactly as today.

(3) Interface and exact values. The existing exports `extractSearchableText(messages)` and `findMatches(extracted, query)` in `src/renderer/features/agents/search/chat-search-utils.ts` keep their signatures. Each entry returned by `extractSearchableText` has `{ messageId, partIndex, partType, text }`.

Unchanged: for a `user` message, all `text` parts with non-whitespace text are joined with `\n`, display markers are stripped as today, and one entry is produced with `partIndex: 0`, `partType: 'text'`. For an assistant message, a `text` part with non-whitespace text yields `{ partType: 'text', text }` at its own index.

New: for each assistant-message part (at its own `partIndex`), the following entries are produced, in this row order within the part, one per field whose value is a string containing at least one non-whitespace character (the text is used exactly as stored, not trimmed):

| part `type` | `partType` of the entry | value |
|---|---|---|
| `tool-Bash` | `tool-Bash:command` | `input.command` |
| `tool-Bash` | `tool-Bash:stdout` | `output.stdout`; if that is missing or empty, `output.output` |
| `tool-Bash` | `tool-Bash:stderr` | `output.stderr` |
| `tool-Read` | `tool-Read:path` | `input.file_path` |
| `tool-Write` | `tool-Write:path` | `input.file_path` |
| `tool-Write` | `tool-Write:content` | `input.content` |
| `tool-Edit` | `tool-Edit:path` | `input.file_path` |
| `tool-Edit` | `tool-Edit:content` | `input.new_string` |
| `tool-Glob` | `tool-Glob:pattern` | `input.pattern` |
| `tool-Grep` | `tool-Grep:pattern` | `input.pattern` |
| `tool-WebSearch` | `tool-WebSearch:query` | `input.query` |
| `tool-WebFetch` | `tool-WebFetch:url` | `input.url` |

Any other part type yields no entries. A field whose `input` or `output` object is missing, or whose value is not a string, yields no entry for that field; the part's other fields are still read. A message without `parts` yields no entries, and a user message's non-text parts contribute nothing. Entries follow message order, then part order. `findMatches` is unchanged: a match in a tool entry carries that entry's `partType`, and its `id` is `` `${messageId}:${partIndex}:${partType}:${offset}` ``.

items.title: Webhook triggers that fire only for chosen assignees
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. A webhook trigger's assignee setting can be 'me', 'anyone' or 'specific' (the editor's AssigneeMode type and its stored-conditions parser both accept 'specific'). A trigger saved with assignee 'specific' fires for every event, whoever the event is assigned to, even unassigned ones. There is also no way to store or read back which people were chosen: the conditions packer never writes them and the editor's parser never returns them.

(2) Required behaviour. 'specific' means "fire only when the event is assigned to one of the chosen people". The chosen person ids are stored on the trigger's conditions under the key `assignee_id`. They must survive a save and reload in the editor. The editor's assignee control must offer the 'specific' choice and a way to enter the ids. A 'specific' trigger with no chosen ids must never fire.

(3) Interface and exact values.
- matchesConditions(conditions, eventData, userExternalId?) (src/shared/lib/webhook-match.ts). The event's assignees are read as today, from eventData.owner_ids or eventData.ownerIds (a single value or an array). When conditions.assignee === 'specific':
  - conditions.assignee_id may be a string or an array of strings. The chosen ids are that string, or the array's string elements, each trimmed, with empty ones dropped.
  - The result is false when there are no chosen ids: assignee_id missing, '', '  ', [], a number, an object, or an array with no non-empty strings.
  - Otherwise the conditions pass the assignee check only when at least one event assignee, converted with String(), equals a chosen id. The comparison is exact and case-sensitive. userExternalId plays no part.
  - All other conditions (from_status, to_status, filters, legacy keys) still apply as today. 'me' and 'anyone' behave exactly as today, and assignee_id is ignored for them.
- packWebhookTriggerConditions(o) (src/shared/lib/webhook-trigger-condition-pack.ts) takes a new optional input field `assigneeIds?: string[]`. When o.supportsAssignee is true and o.assigneeMode === 'specific', the output has assignee: 'specific'. It also has assignee_id: the assigneeIds trimmed, with empties and repeats removed, in first-seen order, but only when at least one id remains. When the mode is not 'specific', or supportsAssignee is false, the output never has an assignee_id key. Everything else in the output is unchanged.
- parseConditions(conditions, eventType, providerId) (src/renderer/lib/flows/webhook-trigger/parse-conditions.ts). The returned WebhookTriggerFormState gains `assigneeIds: string[]`, read from the stored assignee_id: a non-empty trimmed string gives [that string], an array gives its non-empty trimmed string elements in order, and anything else (including missing) gives []. A malformed assignee_id never fails the rest of the parse.
- Round trip: for shortcut story_assigned (an event that supports assignee), packing { assigneeMode: 'specific', assigneeIds: ['u1','u2'], supportsAssignee: true, supportsStateTransition: false, fromStatus: '', toStatus: '', filters: [] } and parsing the result back gives assigneeMode 'specific' and assigneeIds ['u1','u2'].

items.title: Worktree Electron cleanup that also works on Windows
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. `bun run kill:worktree-electron` stops stray Electron processes started from Frink worktrees under ~/.frink/worktrees/frink/<name>/. It does this on macOS and Linux only. On Windows it prints "kill-worktree-electron: not implemented on Windows." and exits without doing anything, although Windows is a supported platform. The rules that decide which processes it stops also cannot be checked without real processes: there is no importable function for them.

(2) Required behaviour. On Windows the command finds and stops the same kind of processes it stops on macOS and Linux: Electron processes whose command line (or, where it can be found, working directory) is inside a Frink worktree. It never stops the main "Frink Dev" app and never touches the main checkout's dev run. Windows paths use backslashes and are case-insensitive, and the Electron binary there is electron.exe. The selection rules below must be available as an importable function whose module has no side effects when imported. macOS and Linux behaviour stays as it is today.

(3) Interface and exact values.
- New export from scripts/lib/worktree-electron-pids.mjs:
  selectWorktreeElectronPids(processes, platform) -> { pids: number[], hintMainDev: boolean }
  processes: Array<{ pid: number, command: string, cwd?: string | null }>. platform: a Node platform string ('darwin', 'linux', 'win32').
  Importing the module must not spawn processes, print anything (console.log, console.error, console.warn) or call process.exit.
- Normalisation. On 'win32' only, command and cwd are compared with every '\' treated as '/', and all checks below (substrings and the pattern) are case-insensitive. On other platforms the checks are case-sensitive and backslashes are left alone, except the 'electron-vite' check, which is always case-insensitive.
- A process is ELECTRON when its command contains any of: 'Electron.app', 'Electron Helper', 'electron-vite', 'node_modules/electron', 'electron/cli.js', '.bin/electron', 'default_app.asar', or it matches /[/\s]Electron(\s|$)/. On 'win32' a command containing 'electron.exe' is also ELECTRON.
- A string is IN_WORKTREE when it contains '.frink/worktrees/frink/' or '/worktrees/frink/' (after the normalisation above).
- A command containing 'Frink Dev' (exact, case-sensitive, on every platform) is never selected and never counts for the hint.
- Selected: ELECTRON and (command IN_WORKTREE, or cwd is a non-empty string IN_WORKTREE). A missing, null or empty cwd never selects. Only positive integer pids can be selected (0, negative and non-integer pids are dropped).
- pids: the selected pids with no repeats, sorted from highest to lowest (for example 5, 900, 42, 900 gives [900, 42, 5]).
- hintMainDev: true only when pids is empty and some process that is not 'Frink Dev' has a command that contains 'electron-vite' (case-insensitive), is ELECTRON and is not IN_WORKTREE (the cwd plays no part in the hint). Otherwise false; an empty process list gives { pids: [], hintMainDev: false }.
- Examples (every backslash below is one literal '\' character in the string): on 'darwin' and 'linux', [{ pid: 101, command: '/Users/a/.frink/worktrees/frink/wt1/node_modules/electron/dist/Electron.app/Contents/MacOS/Electron .' }] gives { pids: [101], hintMainDev: false }; on 'darwin', [{ pid: 300, command: 'node /Users/a/frink/node_modules/.bin/electron-vite dev' }] gives { pids: [], hintMainDev: true }; on 'win32', [{ pid: 203, command: 'C:\x\ELECTRON.EXE --type=renderer', cwd: 'C:\Users\A\.Frink\Worktrees\Frink\wt3\' }] gives pids [203].
- On Windows, running the command must no longer print the "not implemented on Windows." line.

items.title: Go to definition: path aliases in solution-style tsconfig projects and baseUrl-less projects do not resolve
items.brief:
Symptom: in a project whose `tsconfig.json` is a solution file (`{"files": [], "references": [{"path": "./tsconfig.web.json"}, {"path": "./tsconfig.node.json"}]}`, the layout electron-vite and Vite templates generate) with the aliases declared in a referenced config (`tsconfig.web.json`: `{"compilerOptions": {"baseUrl": ".", "paths": {"@/*": ["./src/*"]}}, "include": ["src"]}`), resolving `@/lib/utils` or `@/styles/app.scss` from `src/main.ts` returns `null`, and the project's path-alias lookup returns `{}`. In a project that declares `paths` without `baseUrl` (allowed since TypeScript 4.1), an aliased non-TypeScript import such as `@/styles/app.scss` also resolves to `null`. When two `paths` patterns both match (for example `@/*` and `@/ui/*`), the result depends on key order instead of TypeScript's longest-prefix rule.

Required behaviour:
1. Config selection. The project's candidate root configs are, in order, `tsconfig.json`, `tsconfig.app.json`, `jsconfig.json` in `projectPath` (as today). A root config's `references` entries are followed: each `path` is relative to that config's directory and names either a config file or a directory (meaning `<dir>/tsconfig.json`). "Declares path aliases" means the parsed compiler options (after `extends`) have `baseUrl` or `paths`.
2. `resolveModuleSpecifier(projectPath, containingFile, specifier)` (exported from `src/main/lib/module-resolver.ts`, returns an absolute file path or `null`) resolves with the compiler options of the config that owns `containingFile`: among the first existing root config and the configs it references, the first whose included files (its `files` / `include` / `exclude` as TypeScript computes them) contain `containingFile`. If none contains it, it uses the first of them that declares path aliases; if none declares aliases, it behaves as today. Example: with `tsconfig.node.json` = `{"compilerOptions": {"baseUrl": ".", "paths": {"@main/*": ["src/main/*"]}}, "include": ["src/main/**/*"]}` and `tsconfig.web.json` = `{"compilerOptions": {"baseUrl": ".", "paths": {"@renderer/*": ["src/renderer/src/*"]}}, "include": ["src/renderer/**/*"]}` both referenced from `tsconfig.json`, `@renderer/components/Button` from `src/renderer/src/App.tsx` resolves to `<project>/src/renderer/src/components/Button.tsx` and `@main/ipc` from `src/main/index.ts` resolves to `<project>/src/main/ipc.ts`.
3. Non-TypeScript aliased imports (`.scss`, `.css`, `.json`, `.svg` and the other asset extensions and index files already probed today) resolve through `paths` even when `baseUrl` is not set: targets are relative to the directory of the config file that declares `paths`, as in TypeScript (for `paths` inherited through `extends`, the directory of the extended config file that declares them). With `{"compilerOptions": {"paths": {"@/*": ["./src/*"]}}}`, `@/styles/app.scss` resolves to `<project>/src/styles/app.scss`.
4. When several `paths` patterns match a specifier, the pattern with the longest text before its `*` is tried first; if no file is found through it, the next longest matching pattern is tried. With `{"@/*": ["./src/*"], "@/ui/*": ["./packages/ui/*"]}` and both `src/ui/button.css` and `packages/ui/button.css` present, `@/ui/button.css` resolves to `<project>/packages/ui/button.css` whatever the key order.
5. `resolveTsConfigPaths(projectPath)` (async, exported from `src/main/lib/tsconfig-resolver.ts`, returns `{ baseUrl?, paths? }`): when the root config declares no aliases it looks through that config's `references` in order and returns the first referenced config's aliases (if neither the root config nor any referenced config declares aliases, the next candidate is tried as today), with `baseUrl` being the config's `baseUrl` as TypeScript resolves it (an absolute path) when set and otherwise the directory of that config file (the same fallback used today). For the solution-style project in the symptom it returns `paths` `{"@/*": ["./src/*"]}` and `baseUrl` equal to the project directory.
6. Projects that resolve today keep resolving the same way. Existing tests must keep passing; `clearResolverCache()` still clears any cached config state.

items.title: Ghost Run pre-flight reports the structural problems a real run rejects
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. Ghost Run (Rehearse) is meant to warn about everything that would stop a flow before it runs, but its static analysis (`analyzeFlow`) only checks node settings, missing condition branches, unreachable steps and template references. Graphs that the run-time validator refuses in run mode come back from Ghost Run with no finding at all, for example: a trigger wired to two first steps, an End step with an outgoing edge, a Run Command step with two outgoing edges, a loop that goes back through a non-condition step, a condition whose true and false branches both loop back, a condition with `loop.maxIterations: 0`, and a Fan Out with `mode: 'burst'` or `maxParallel: 20`. The user sees a clean rehearsal and then the run fails.

(2) Required behaviour. `analyzeFlow` also reports these structural problems, each as a finding attached to the offending node, so a rehearsal that comes back clean is not refused by the run-time validator for any of these reasons.

(3) Interface and exact values. `analyzeFlow(graph: FlowGraph, customNodeInputs?)` from src/renderer/lib/flow-rehearsal/analyze.ts keeps its signature and `RehearsalFinding` shape (nodeId, nodeLabel, severity, rule, why, fix; why and fix are non-empty plain-English strings whose wording is up to you). New findings, all with severity 'error':
- rule 'trigger.edge_count' on the trigger node when it has more than one outgoing edge, or has no outgoing edge while the graph contains at least one other node. A graph that holds only a trigger (and the empty graph) stays clean.
- rule 'end.has_outgoing' on an `end` node that has one or more outgoing edges.
- rule 'node.too_many_outgoing' on any node that is not the trigger, not `condition`, not `fan_out` and not `end`, when it has more than one outgoing edge.
- rule 'node.cycle' on the source node of an edge that closes a cycle (walking the graph depth-first from the trigger, an edge whose target is already on the current path), when that source node is not a `condition`. Loop-backs from a condition node never produce 'node.cycle'.
- rule 'condition.no_exit' on a `condition` node whose 'true' edge and 'false' edge both close a cycle in that sense. A condition with only one looping branch gets no 'condition.no_exit'.
- rule 'condition.invalid_loop_config' (one finding per node at most) on a `condition` node whose config has a `loop` key and either `loop` is not a plain object, or `loop.maxIterations` is not an integer from 1 to 50, or `loop.onMaxReached` is present and is neither 'fail' nor 'continue'. A condition with no `loop` key, or with `loop: { maxIterations: 5 }` or `loop: { maxIterations: 50, onMaxReached: 'continue' }`, gets no such finding.
- rule 'fan_out.invalid_mode' on a `fan_out` node whose config `mode` is set to anything other than 'sequential' or 'parallel'.
- rule 'fan_out.invalid_max_parallel' on a `fan_out` node whose `mode` is 'parallel' and whose `maxParallel` is present but not an integer from 1 to 10. `maxParallel` is ignored when mode is not 'parallel'.
Findings stay sorted as today (by nodeId, then rule). Existing rules and their results are unchanged, and all existing flow-rehearsal tests keep passing (in particular the empty graph and a lone trigger stay clean, and the existing clean trigger -> start_task -> agent flow still yields zero findings).

Example graphs and the findings they give (node ids in quotes; `rc` means `{ blockType: 'run_command', config: { command: 'echo hi' } }`; the trigger is `{ id: 't', blockType: 'manual_trigger' }` and is listed first):
- t -> 'a' (rc) and t -> 'b' (rc): 'trigger.edge_count' on 't'.
- nodes t, 'a' (rc) with no edges: 'trigger.edge_count' on 't'.
- t -> 'e' (end) -> 'a' (rc): 'end.has_outgoing' on 'e'.
- t -> 'a' (rc), 'a' -> 'b' (rc), 'a' -> 'c' (rc): 'node.too_many_outgoing' on 'a'.
- t -> 'a' (rc) -> 'b' (rc) -> 'a': 'node.cycle' on 'b' and on no other node.
- t -> 'a' (rc) -> 'b' (rc) -> 'cond' (condition), cond --true--> 'a', cond --false--> 'b': 'condition.no_exit' on 'cond'; no 'node.cycle' finding anywhere.
- t -> 'a' (rc) -> 'cond', cond --true--> 'a', cond --false--> 'x' (end): no 'condition.no_exit' and no 'node.cycle'.
- condition configs `{ loop: 'yes' }`, `{ loop: { maxIterations: 0 } }`, `{ loop: { maxIterations: 51 } }`, `{ loop: { maxIterations: 2.5 } }`, `{ loop: { maxIterations: 3, onMaxReached: 'retry' } }` each give exactly one 'condition.invalid_loop_config' on that node.
- fan_out configs `{ mode: 'burst' }` gives 'fan_out.invalid_mode'; `{ mode: 'parallel', maxParallel: 20 }` and `{ mode: 'parallel', maxParallel: 0 }` give 'fan_out.invalid_max_parallel'; `{ mode: 'sequential', maxParallel: 20 }` and `{ mode: 'parallel', maxParallel: 10 }` give neither.

items.title: Unique labels for same-named projects and editor tabs
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. In the code editor, two open files with the same name (for example src/a/index.ts and src/b/index.ts) get identical "index.ts" tabs with nothing to tell them apart. The project labels on the tab bar's project separators, built by `disambiguateProjectPaths`, only ever prepend one parent folder, so '/a/work/api' and '/b/work/api' both come out as 'work/api'. `getProjectName` also returns '' for a path with a trailing separator ('/work/api/') and returns the whole string for a Windows path ('C:\work\api'). The worktree picker's labels have the same one-level limit.

(2) Required behaviour. Labels built from paths are always distinct: when names collide, each one is extended with just enough parent folders to tell it apart. Same-named editor tabs get a short parent-folder hint shown next to the file name, and the worktree picker uses the same labelling rule.

(3) Interface and exact values. Throughout, a path is split into segments on both '/' and '\', and empty segments (from leading or trailing separators) are ignored. Labels and hints join segments with '/'.

a) `getProjectName(projectPath: string | undefined): string | undefined`, exported from src/renderer/lib/code-editor/tabs/project-name.ts (and src/renderer/lib/code-editor/tabs/index.ts): the last segment. getProjectName(undefined) is undefined; getProjectName('/home/dev/work/api') === 'api'; getProjectName('api') === 'api'; getProjectName('/work/api/') === 'api'; getProjectName('C:\work\api') === 'api'.

b) `disambiguateProjectPaths(projectPaths: string[]): Map<string, string>`, same modules, keyed by each input string exactly as given. A path whose last segment is unique among the inputs is labelled with that segment. When several inputs share a last segment, each of them is labelled with its shortest run of trailing segments that no other input in the list also ends with (segment-wise); a path that has no such run is labelled with the full path exactly as given. Exact values:
- ['/work/api', '/work/web'] gives 'api' and 'web'.
- ['/work/api', '/personal/api'] gives 'work/api' and 'personal/api'.
- ['/api', '/work/api'] gives '/api' and 'work/api'.
- ['/a/work/api', '/b/work/api'] gives 'a/work/api' and 'b/work/api'.
- ['/a/work/api', '/b/work/api', '/c/home/api'] gives 'a/work/api', 'b/work/api' and 'home/api'.
- ['C:\work\api', 'D:\home\api'] gives 'work/api' and 'home/api'.
- ['/work/api/', '/home/api'] gives 'work/api' and 'home/api'.
- [] gives an empty map.

c) New export `getFileTabHints(paths: string[]): Map<string, string>`, importable from src/renderer/lib/code-editor/tabs (its index.ts). Input: the absolute paths of the open editor files (a path listed twice counts once). The result has an entry only for paths whose file name (last segment) is shared with at least one other distinct input path; paths with a unique file name have no entry. The hint for such a path is the rule in (b) applied to the parent directories (the path minus its last segment) of the paths in that same-file-name group: the shortest run of trailing parent-directory segments that no other parent directory in the group also ends with, or the full parent directory as given when there is none. Exact values:
- ['/p/src/a/index.ts', '/p/src/b/index.ts', '/p/src/app.ts'] gives '/p/src/a/index.ts' -> 'a' and '/p/src/b/index.ts' -> 'b', and no entry for '/p/src/app.ts'.
- ['/p/x/lib/util.ts', '/p/y/lib/util.ts'] gives 'x/lib' and 'y/lib'.
- ['/p/README.md', '/p/docs/README.md'] gives 'p' and 'docs'.
- ['C:\r\a\index.ts', 'C:\r\b\index.ts'] gives 'a' and 'b'.
- ['/p/src/index.ts', '/p/src/index.ts'] gives an empty map.

d) The editor tab bar shows a tab's hint (dimmed, after the file name) when it has one, and the worktree picker labels non-main worktrees with the rule in (b). All existing tests keep passing.

items.title: In-chat search: counts that match the highlights, plus Match case and Whole word
items.brief:
(1) Symptom. In a chat's search bar (Cmd+F), the match count and the highlights disagree whenever matches can overlap: searching 'aa' in a message containing 'aaaa' reports 3 matches, but only 2 are highlighted, so stepping to the third match highlights nothing. The reported offsets can also be wrong after some non-ASCII characters (for example after 'İ'), so the wrong text is highlighted. The file-content search in the Files sidebar already offers Match case and Whole word toggles; chat search has neither. (2) Required behaviour. Chat search finds non-overlapping matches, the rendered highlights come from the same matching rules as the count, and the search bar offers Match case and Whole word toggles that change both. (3) Interface and exact values. a) `findMatches(extractedTexts, query, options?)` in src/renderer/features/agents/search/chat-search-utils.ts, where `options` is `{ matchCase?: boolean; wholeWord?: boolean }` (both default false). Returned `SearchMatch` objects keep today's shape and id format `${messageId}:${partIndex}:${partType}:${offset}`, with `length` equal to `query.length`; matches are ordered by entry, then offset. Rules: - A query that is empty or only whitespace gives []. The query is matched as typed (not trimmed). - Matches never overlap: after a match at offset i, the search continues at i + query.length. - Without matchCase, letter case is ignored; offsets always index into the entry's original text. With matchCase, comparison is exact. - With wholeWord, a candidate counts only if the character just before it (if any) and the character just after it (if any) are not word characters (a Unicode letter, a Unicode digit, or '_'). A rejected candidate does not consume text: the search continues from the next character. Exact values, for one entry `{ messageId: 'm1', partIndex: 0, partType: 'text', text }`: - text 'aaaa', query 'aa': offsets [0, 2], ids 'm1:0:text:0' and 'm1:0:text:2', each with length 2. - text 'Cat concat cat', query 'cat': offsets [0, 7, 11] (the same with options `{}`); with wholeWord [0, 11]; with matchCase [7, 11]; with both [11], and that match is exactly `{ id: 'm1:0:text:11', messageId: 'm1', partIndex: 0, partType: 'text', offset: 11, length: 3 }`. - text 'catcat cat', query 'cat', wholeWord: offsets [7]. Text 'ba a a', query 'a a', wholeWord: offsets [3]. - query 'cat' with wholeWord: text 'écat cat' gives [5]; text '1cat cat_ cat' gives [10]; text '(cat).' gives [1]. - text 'İx foo', query 'foo': offsets [3], length 3. - query ' ' on text 'a b', and query '' on text 'abc': []. Text 'foo bar', query ' bar': offsets [3]. - two entries, `{ messageId: 'm1', partIndex: 0, text: 'x cat cat' }` then `{ messageId: 'm2', partIndex: 3, text: 'cat' }` (partType 'text'), query 'cat': ids 'm1:0:text:2', 'm1:0:text:6', 'm2:3:text:0', in that order. b) New export `highlightSearchMatchesInDom(container: HTMLElement, query: string, currentMatchIndex: number | null, options?)` from a new module src/renderer/features/agents/search/highlight-dom.ts, with the same `options` type. It: - first removes every existing `mark.search-highlight` inside `container`, putting its text back and merging that text with the neighbouring text nodes, so that text split up by an earlier call is searched as one text node, calling it repeatedly never nests marks, and `container.textContent` is unchanged by any call; - then, for each text node under `container` in document order, finds matches in that node's text with exactly the rules in (a) and wraps each one in a `` holding the original matched text; - adds the class `search-highlight-current` to the mark whose 0-based position among the marks it created equals `currentMatchIndex`; - returns the number of marks it created (0 for an empty or whitespace-only query). Exact values: on `

aaaa

` with query 'aa' it returns 2 and both marks read 'aa'. On `

Cat concat

cat

` with query 'cat', currentMatchIndex 1 and `{ wholeWord: true }` it returns 2, the marks read 'Cat' and 'cat', only the second has `search-highlight-current`, and the div's textContent is still 'Cat concatcat'; calling it again on the same div with query '' returns 0, leaves no mark elements and the same textContent. On `

aaaa

` with currentMatchIndex null, no mark has `search-highlight-current` and the container's textContent stays 'aaaa'. On one container holding `

Cat concat cat

`, successive calls give: query 'cat', currentMatchIndex 0 -> 3; query 'cat', currentMatchIndex 2 -> 3; query 'at', null -> 3, with marks reading 'at', 'at', 'at' and no mark inside another mark; query 'cat', currentMatchIndex 0, `{ matchCase: true }` -> 2, with marks reading 'cat', 'cat' and only the first marked current; query ' ' -> 0, with no mark elements left; the textContent stays 'Cat concat cat' throughout. c) New export `chatSearchOptionsAtom` from src/renderer/features/agents/search/chat-search-atoms.ts: a writable jotai atom whose initial value is `{ matchCase: false, wholeWord: false }` (read through a jotai store; after setting `{ matchCase: true, wholeWord: false }` through the same store, reading it gives that value). d) The chat search bar shows Match case and Whole word toggles bound to `chatSearchOptionsAtom`; changing them re-runs the search, and the highlights shown in rendered assistant text and in user message bubbles follow the same rules and the same options as the count, so the count and the highlights always agree. All existing tests keep passing.
